quote: Grundproblem der Reduction besteht darin n lineare Formen
english: The basic problem of reduction consists in [taking] n linear forms
topic: The page concludes an argument that a function which is rational in y for each x (and conversely) and continuous in x is a rational function of x and y, then begins stating the basic problem of reduction of n linear forms.

triage.modern_statement: The note breaks off after the setup: 'the basic problem of reduction consists in [taking] n linear forms ...'. The actual task is never stated, so the exact question can't be recovered. In 19th-century arithmetic, 'reduction' of n linear forms in n variables usually meant this. Take real forms L_i = a_i1 x_1 + ... + a_in x_n (i = 1..n) with nonzero determinant. Apply an integer unimodular change of variables (equivalently, change the basis of the lattice they define) to bring them into a 'reduced' normal form with small coefficients. A related goal is finding nonzero integer points where all |L_i(x)| are small. This is the reduction theory of Hermite and Minkowski, also stated for the positive quadratic form ΣL_i². That reading is my inference from the words used and is not stated on the page.

If it means the classical reduction problem for n linear forms (equivalently positive definite quadratic forms or lattice bases): Hermite started it in his letters to Jacobi (published 1850). Minkowski developed it in his reduction theory and Geometry of Numbers, including the linear forms theorem. Korkine–Zolotarev added a further reduction notion, and the field continues today in lattice basis reduction algorithms. Sources do not tie this particular Hilbert note to any specific later result.

evidence.claim: Hermite described the first reduction algorithms in arbitrary dimension in his letters to Jacobi, in the language of quadratic forms.
In his 1850 letters to Jacobi, Hermite treated forms with any number of indeterminates and real coefficients.

The classical reductions of positive n-ary quadratic forms (lattice bases) are those of Hermite, Minkowski and Korkine–Zolotarev, and they are still studied (e.g. equivalence of reduction domains in low dimensions).
Minkowski's linear forms theorem is set up for n real linear forms in n variables with nonzero determinant, the same 'n linear forms' setting as Hilbert's note.
Related problems about n linear forms remain open, e.g. Minkowski's conjecture on products of n inhomogeneous linear forms.
